response: {"turns":[{"id":"M1:T101","text":"Generally that means a whole stack of protections: mechanical hard stops, electrical interlocks, electrical hard limit switches, soft limit switches, software limits, and watchdogs."},{"id":"M1:T102","text":"And the safety aspects need to be analyzed during the functional specification phase of the software. On security, we need it for two things. One, to stop commands from different users on different parts of the system getting accidentally mixed up. Two, to keep anyone from the wide area network from getting into the Gemini 8m Telescopes."},{"id":"M1:T103","text":"Got it."},{"id":"M1:T104","text":"The astronomical database especially has to be protected from intrusion, whether someone's after private data or just trying to do damage."},{"id":"M1:T105","text":"Okay, let's switch to testability. How are we thinking about testing?"},{"id":"M1:T106","text":"There'll be a plan, and it covers every area of testing: design, acceptance, commissioning, all the way through to hand-over."},{"id":"M1:T107","text":"Great. What about modularity, how should the system be split up?"},{"id":"M1:T108","text":"Well, alongside that, you still need to be able to get information about other parts of the system, telescope coordinates for example. That ties back to the control flow requirements in Section 3.1.1."},{"id":"M1:T109","text":"Next, installation aspects. Anything we need to keep in mind there?"},{"id":"M1:T110","text":"So every system has to be able to report its current version when you ask for it."},{"id":"M1:T111","text":"Let's talk remote operations. How do you see that working?"},{"id":"M1:T112","text":"We'd need some kind of security controlling access to system features. Maybe some operations only allowed from specific remote sites, like Hale Pohaku or Hilo in Hawaii, Cerro Tololo in Chile, places like that."},{"id":"M1:T113","text":"Okay."},{"id":"M1:T114","text":"Anything else on remote operations?"},{"id":"M1:T115","text":"No, that's it."},{"id":"M1:T116","text":"Then let's move on to normal operation. What does a typical day look like?"},{"id":"M1:T117","text":"Start with start-up and shut-down. There are procedures at a bunch of different levels. Cold start-up, so from scratch including downloading all the software, should take about 5 minutes, and that doesn't count starting the telescope or instruments. Warm start-up is from scratch but without the software download, about 1 minute. Telescope start-up, counted from the end of cold or warm start-up, should be about 4 minutes. Then instrument start-up, from the end of telescope start-up, 2 minutes or less. We also need a way to shut down all subsystems, hardware and software. And every start-up and shut-down gets logged automatically with time stamps, so we can do statistics on system availability."},{"id":"M1:T118","text":"Makes sense."},{"id":"M1:T119","text":"Then engineering logging. We need to log engineering data at rates up to 200 Hz for short periods, and that data has to be available to external software packages for analysis. For long-term logging, slower rates, 1 Hz or less, into a common format, which is baselined as SYBASE."},{"id":"M1:T120","text":"Okay. And what about operation in failure mode? What should happen when things go wrong?"}]}
